questions.question: What is the starting point of the stack walkthrough?
options: A) An unread message inside an Ethernet switch
B) A physical signal without an application
C) A running SMTP process
D) A MAC address stored in DNS
questions.explanation: The process creates the application data and uses the stack to communicate.

questions.question: What does a socket provide to the SMTP process?
options: A) A path that bypasses TCP and IP
B) An interface for sending and receiving data through the operating system
C) The recipient mailbox password
D) The physical cable between two routers
questions.explanation: The socket is the local application interface to transport communication.

questions.question: Why does a sending mail server query DNS MX records?
options: A) To discover a remote MAC address across the Internet
B) To encrypt the message body
C) To decide whether Bob has read the message
D) To find the recipient domain mail server
questions.explanation: MX records identify mail exchanger names; address lookups provide IP addresses.

questions.question: Which protocol defines commands such as EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, and DATA?
options: A) IP
B) ARP
C) SMTP
D) Ethernet
questions.explanation: SMTP defines the application conversation for transferring the message.

questions.question: What does TCP contribute to the message journey?
options: A) The recipient domain MX record
B) A complete mailbox reading interface
C) An ordered reliable byte stream between endpoints
D) The MAC forwarding table of every switch
questions.explanation: TCP detects missing data and can retransmit it while delivering bytes in order.

questions.question: What is the usual order of the TCP handshake?
options: A) DATA, SYN, QUIT
B) SYN, SYN ACK, ACK
C) ARP, MX, DATA
D) ACK, FIN, EHLO
questions.explanation: The three-way handshake establishes TCP connection state before the ordinary SMTP exchange.

questions.question: Which sequence describes the sending stack?
options: A) SMTP bytes, TCP segment, IP packet, link frame, signals
B) Signals, IP packet, SMTP bytes, link frame, TCP segment
C) SMTP bytes, DNS record, ARP message, mailbox
D) TCP segment, SMTP bytes, signals, IP packet, link frame
questions.explanation: Each lower layer wraps and carries the data supplied by the layer above it.

questions.question: What is encapsulation?
options: A) Adding the protocol information needed as data travels down the stack
B) Opening a mailbox in a browser
C) Removing every header at a switch
D) Replacing the recipient address with a DNS query
questions.explanation: TCP, IP, and link processing add information for their respective delivery functions.

questions.question: Which address remains the IP destination when the sender sends a frame to its gateway?
options: A) The gateway MAC address
B) The visible email To field
C) The remote mail server IP address
D) The switch port number
questions.explanation: The frame targets the local next hop while the packet targets the remote host.

questions.question: What does ARP discover in the IPv4 example?
options: A) The remote SMTP password
B) The recipient domain MX preference
C) The complete Internet route
D) A local next hop MAC address
questions.explanation: ARP resolves a neighbor on the current link; IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly describes switches and routers?
options: A) Switches forward local frames; routers forward IP packets between networks
B) Switches interpret SMTP; routers read mailboxes
C) Switches resolve DNS; routers assign message subjects
D) Switches establish TCP; routers replace TCP with SMTP
questions.explanation: Switching uses local MAC forwarding; routing connects IP networks.

questions.question: What happens to link framing at a forwarding router?
options: A) The same frame carries the same MAC addresses over every routed link
B) The router removes the incoming frame and creates an outgoing frame
C) The router converts the SMTP message into an MX record
D) The router must become the final SMTP recipient
questions.explanation: Link encapsulation belongs to each local delivery step, not the full routed path.

questions.question: What happens as the message travels up the receiving stack?
options: A) Link information is removed, IP hands data to TCP, and TCP supplies bytes to SMTP
B) SMTP parses the Ethernet signals before TCP sees them
C) The switch writes the message directly into the mailbox
D) The receiving host repeats the sender DNS query for every byte
questions.explanation: Decapsulation and transport reconstruction make application bytes available through the socket.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a TCP ACK from SMTP acceptance?
options: A) A TCP ACK proves that Bob read the message
B) An SMTP success replaces all TCP acknowledgments
C) The two replies always mean exactly the same thing
D) A TCP ACK confirms stream receipt; a final SMTP success after content confirms application acceptance
questions.explanation: Different layers confirm different events; neither reply proves that the recipient has read the email.

questions.question: Which OSI layer corresponds to IP?
options: A) Presentation
B) Network
C) Session
D) Physical
questions.explanation: IP handles addressing and forwarding across networks at OSI layer 3.

questions.question: How does the receiving server send an SMTP reply?
options: A) It bypasses the network because a connection already exists
B) It is delivered by DNS instead of TCP
C) It is stored only in the local Ethernet switch
D) Its reply travels down its stack and back up the sender stack
questions.explanation: Replies require the same layered transport and network delivery as commands.
